source_text: Circa officia uero priuatarum et communium sollemnitatum, ut togae purae, ut sponsalium, ut nuptialium, ut nominalium, nullum putem periculum obseruari de flatu idololatriae, quae interuenit. causae enim sunt considerandae, quibus praestatur officium. eas mundas esse opinor per semetipsas, quia neque uestitus uirilis neque anulus aut coniunctio maritalis de alicuius idoli honore descendit. nullum denique cultum a deo maledictum inuenio, nisi muliebrem in uiro. maledictus enim, inquit, omnis qui muliebribus induitur. toga uero etiam appellatione uirilis est. nuptias quoque celebrari non magis deus prohibet quam nomen imponi. sed his accommodantur sacrificia. sim uocatus nec adsacrificii sit titulus officii, et operae meae expunctio quantum sibi libet. utinam quidem nec uidere possimus quae facere nobis nefas est. sed quoniam ita malus circumdedit saeculum idololatria, licebit adesse in quibusdam, quae nos homini, non idolo, officiosos habent. plane ad sacerdotium et sacrificium uocatus non ibo (proprium enim idoli officium est), sed neque consilio neque sumptu aliaue opera in eiusmodi fungar. si propter sacrificium uocatus adsistam, ero particeps idololatriae: si me alia causa coniungit sacrificanti, ero tantum spectator sacrificii.
thought_title: Private and common ceremonies: when attendance is safe
orientation: Tertullian is now applying his rule about idolatry to private and common social ceremonies, distinguishing the ceremony itself from the sacrifices attached to it.
pass_a_gloss: But concerning the duties of private and common ceremonies, such as the toga of manhood, such as betrothals, such as weddings, such as name-days, I would think there is no danger to be guarded against from the breath of idolatry, which comes in between. For the causes must be considered, for which the duty is performed. I think these are pure in themselves, because neither the manly garment nor the ring or the marital union descends from the honor of any idol. In short, I find no dress cursed by God, except womanly dress on a man. For cursed, he says, is everyone who is clothed in womanly things. But the toga is manly even by its name. God does not forbid weddings to be celebrated any more than a name to be given. But sacrifices are attached to these things. If I am invited and the title of the duty is not that of sacrifice, let the discharge of my service be as much as it likes. Would that indeed we could not even see the things which it is unlawful for us to do. But since the evil one has surrounded the world with idolatry, it will be allowed to be present at certain things which hold us as dutiful to a man, not to an idol. Clearly, if I am invited to a priesthood and sacrifice, I will not go (for that is the proper duty of an idol), but neither will I serve in such a thing by counsel or by expense or by any other work. If I am invited for the sake of sacrifice and I stand by, I will be a partaker of idolatry: if another cause joins me to the one sacrificing, I will be only a spectator of the sacrifice.

choices.why: Keeps the metaphor of idolatry as a contaminating breath or vapor that can touch even innocent ceremonies.
The toga pura was the plain white toga assumed by Roman boys at coming of age; 'of manhood' conveys the rite of passage.
Nominalia were ceremonies for naming a child; 'name-days' is the standard English term for this Roman custom.
Expunctio is a bookkeeping term for marking off a completed item; 'discharge' preserves the sense of fulfilling a social obligation.
Officiosus means acting from duty or obligation; the phrase means these occasions make us dutiful to a person, not an idol.
Particeps means sharing in something; 'partaker' preserves the sense of sharing guilt by participation.

bible_refs.note: maledictus enim, inquit, omnis qui muliebribus induitur

pass_b_english: Now consider the duties attached to private and common ceremonies: the toga of manhood, betrothals, weddings, name-days. I think there is no danger to be feared from the breath of idolatry that touches them. For we must consider the reasons for which the duty is performed. These I consider clean in themselves, because neither a man's dress nor a ring nor the union of marriage derives from the honor of any idol. In fact, I find no dress cursed by God except a woman's dress on a man. For it says, "Cursed is everyone who wears women's clothing" (Deuteronomy 22:5). The toga, however, is even called by a man's name. God no more forbids celebrating weddings than he does giving a name. But sacrifices are attached to these occasions. If I am invited, let the occasion not be titled as a sacrifice, and let the discharge of my service be as much as I choose. I wish indeed that we could not even see what we are forbidden to do. But since the evil one has surrounded the world with idolatry, it will be permitted to be present at certain things that hold us as dutiful to a person, not to an idol. If I am invited to a priesthood or a sacrifice, I will not go, for that is the proper duty of an idol. But neither will I serve in such a thing by counsel, by expense, or by any other work. If I am invited for the sake of a sacrifice and I attend, I will be a partaker of idolatry; if another reason joins me to the one sacrificing, I will be only a spectator of the sacrifice.

last_rejected.quote: In fact, I find no dress cursed by God except a woman's dress on a man.
last_rejected.source_quote: nullum denique cultum a deo maledictum inuenio, nisi muliebrem in uiro.
last_rejected.why: Latin says “cultum” (worship/ritual), not “dress”; the translation changes the object of God’s curse.
last_rejected.fix: In fact, I find no worship cursed by God except a woman's dress on a man.
last_rejected.ruling: cultus means 'dress/clothing' here; context (vestitus, muliebribus induitur) confirms 'dress,' not 'worship.'

polish.changed: Clarified the opening list by removing the dash and making the sentence flow naturally, and adjusted punctuation around the refusal to attend a priesthood or sacrifice so the reason reads as a clear explanatory clause rather than an aside.

notes.why: Roman coming-of-age ceremony with religious overtones; needs context.
notes.fix: Note: 'toga of manhood = toga virilis, assumed at Roman coming-of-age.'
